title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
insight: Incumbents who vote against their party more often outperform electorally, other factors equal.
evidence: Roll-call loyalty over past three Congresses.
forecasting_implication: Use party-loyalty scores for incumbents.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
insight: Greater polarization produces closer margins and smaller effects of the economy and incumbency.

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
insight: US polls considerably understated Republican performance in several recent elections.
forecasting_implication: Systematic error can recur in the same direction across cycles. Models should allow correlated, election-wide polling error, and pollster ratings should account for it.

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
insight: Many pollsters have strong political opinions and ties to operatives, and some poll for campaigns. Partisan ties alone do not establish inaccuracy.
evidence: Silver's experience with the FiveThirtyEight pollster ledger.
forecasting_implication: Measure pollster bias empirically through house effects rather than inferring it from affiliations.

title: Is a Trump-Biden rematch inevitable?
insight: A primary challenger needs an identifiable factional coalition to be viable. Pat Buchanan had staunch conservatives in 1992; RFK Jr. lacks any Democratic faction. Even Buchanan peaked in New Hampshire, just under 40%, and lost every state.
evidence: Buchanan never got more than 36% after New Hampshire.
forecasting_implication: A surprising early showing by a factionless protest candidate should not move nomination odds much.

title: Is a Trump-Biden rematch inevitable?
insight: Candidates can poll decently early because of name recognition, then fade as voters learn their positions. RFK Jr. ended up viewed more favorably by Republicans than by Democrats.
evidence: Kennedy's RCP average declined from about 20 to 11.9 between May and September 2023.
forecasting_implication: Discount early polling of well-known names whose positions clash with the party base.

title: Is a Trump-Biden rematch inevitable?
insight: Late entrants to nomination races face huge obstacles in money, staff and message. Bloomberg entered in November 2019 and flopped despite unlimited resources.
evidence: Bloomberg's 2020 campaign won only American Samoa.
forecasting_implication: The probability of a late-entrant victory should be low, and it falls as the calendar advances.

title: Is a Trump-Biden rematch inevitable?
insight: If an incumbent withdraws late, the vice president is the most likely replacement. In a chaotic rump process, name recognition and incumbency status matter more than electoral track record.
forecasting_implication: In replacement scenarios, weight the designated or likely successor heavily.

title: Is a Trump-Biden rematch inevitable?
insight: Silver says LBJ's 1968 withdrawal reflected ideological vulnerability (Vietnam). Biden's weakness is concentrated on age, not ideology, because he calibrates well between party flanks.
evidence: In the CNN poll, 49% cited age as their biggest concern about Biden.
forecasting_implication: Concerns limited to age do not create an opening for an ideological challenger.

title: Is a Trump-Biden rematch inevitable?
insight: Republican primary voters had not shown concern about Trump's indictments, but swing voters might care about a conviction even if partisans don't.
forecasting_implication: Model scandal effects differently for primary electorates and general electorates.

title: Is a Trump-Biden rematch inevitable?
insight: Parties have a long history of not renominating losing candidates. Trump is an exception because most Republicans believe the 2020 election was stolen.
forecasting_implication: Historical base rates can fail when the electorate rejects the premise behind them.

title: Is a Trump-Biden rematch inevitable?
insight: A 45% general-election win chance for a challenger against an incumbent is, in Silver's view, pretty high.
forecasting_implication: This implies an incumbency prior favoring the incumbent.

title: The election model is a little too popular
insight: As of September 2023, Silver saw a Trump-Biden rematch as likely, with possibly neither primary competitive. He expected a potentially very close election lasting another 14 months, with few new day-to-day storylines.
forecasting_implication: A long, stable rematch campaign may mean low poll volatility while public attention to every small shift stays intense.

title: The election model is a little too popular

forecasting_implication: Expect polling accuracy debates to be politicized, especially around populist candidates.

title: The incumbency advantage is disappearing. Maybe it's the algorithms' fault.
insight: Being an incumbent president no longer confers a large popular-vote edge. Recent incumbents' margins fluctuate around zero, compared with a +10.3 average in 1948-1984.
evidence: Margins of the last five incumbents: -5.6, +8.5, +2.4, +3.7, -4.5. A linear trend turns negative by 2020.
forecasting_implication: Fundamentals models should give a much smaller incumbency bonus than older regressions imply, possibly near zero, and perhaps let it vary by era.

title: The incumbency advantage is disappearing. Maybe it's the algorithms' fault.
insight: Higher partisanship and fewer swing voters shrink the variance of presidential margins compared with mid-20th-century landslides.
evidence: Margins in 1948-1984 ranged from -9.7 to +23.2. Recent margins are within about ±9.
forecasting_implication: Priors on national margin dispersion should be narrower in the polarized era.

title: The incumbency advantage is disappearing. Maybe it's the algorithms' fault.
insight: Incumbents across democracies of all ideologies are unpopular and losing elections, so Biden's unpopularity is not unusual. The trend is arguably stronger in English-speaking countries and for left-leaning parties.
evidence: Trudeau's polling, UK Conservatives' polling, New Zealand's center-left losing in 2023, Australia's conservatives ousted in 2022 (citing Yglesias).
forecasting_implication: There may be a cross-national anti-incumbent environment that weighs on incumbents beyond domestic fundamentals.

title: The incumbency advantage is disappearing. Maybe it's the algorithms' fault.
insight: Strategic retirements by incumbents expecting to lose (e.g., Manchin) and fewer competitive seats inflate Congressional reelection rates. The underlying Congressional incumbency advantage has declined.
evidence: Regression controlling for these factors, per Silver; details not shown.
forecasting_implication: House and Senate models should treat open seats created by retirements as signals and use a smaller incumbency coefficient.

title: The incumbency advantage is disappearing. Maybe it's the algorithms' fault.
insight: Algorithmic, competitive media and social media reward negative emotional content. That negativity motivates both clicks and voting, which hurts incumbents. Silver notes the incumbency advantage was high in the curated 'objective journalism' era from post-WWII to the early 1990s, and low in the yellow-journalism era.
evidence: He reports the timing correlation with the incumbency chart; this is a qualitative argument.
forecasting_implication: A structural reason to expect the incumbency penalty to persist or worsen.

title: The incumbency advantage is disappearing. Maybe it's the algorithms' fault.

forecasting_implication: Measures of inflation and economic sentiment may predict incumbent performance better than employment data alone.

evidence: Strong Democratic performance in special elections; Biden doing slightly better in likely-voter than registered-voter polls in 2024.

title: 2024 presidential election model methodology update

evidence: RFK Jr. fell from around 10% to the mid-to-high single digits.

title: 2024 presidential election model methodology update
insight: Presidential rematches show high persistence in results.
evidence: 1952/1956 Eisenhower-Stevenson and 1896/1900 McKinley-Bryan had similar maps; Cleveland won the popular vote narrowly against Harrison in both 1888 and 1892.
forecasting_implication: Reduce uncertainty and increase weight on the prior result in rematches.

title: 2024 presidential election model methodology update
insight: High polarization shrinks the incumbency advantage, makes elections tighter, and reduces convention bounces.
evidence: Voteview data; modest recent bounces.
forecasting_implication: Scale fundamentals effects and bounces down when polarization is high.

title: 2024 presidential election model methodology update
insight: Reallocated votes in ranked-choice elections often do not split evenly between the major candidates.
forecasting_implication: Randomize the reallocation splits.

title: The presidential election isn't a toss-up

forecasting_implication: Shrink incumbency effects and fundamentals-based margins in polarized eras.

evidence: Bush was an incumbent, and the economy was doing decently; Bush won by a mere 2 points.
forecasting_implication: A baseline for what average candidate quality looks like relative to fundamentals.

title: The broken leg problem
insight: A candidate visibly unable to campaign (Biden at 81 after the debate) likely underperforms what historically trained models assume, and voters recognize it.
evidence: Debate performance, reliance on teleprompters, verbal stumbles, and loss of party confidence.
forecasting_implication: Candidate-specific capability shocks may warrant downward qualitative adjustments beyond what the model captures.

title: The broken leg problem

forecasting_implication: Expect circumstances outside the training data.

insight: Compared with Biden, Harris gained more among young voters and voters of color and less among older white voters. This hurts her relative position in states like Wisconsin, which have many older white voters.
evidence: Biden's numbers held up better with old white voters.
forecasting_implication: Demographic composition shifts change state relative leans and the size of the Electoral College bias.

title: The Electoral College bias has returned with a vengeance
insight: The honeymoon enthusiasm after the Biden-to-Harris switch likely inflated Democratic polling through differential response. That inflation is cooling as both parties become equally enthused.
forecasting_implication: Expect reversion after enthusiasm surges.

title: Oops! I made the convention bounce adjustment disappear.
insight: Without Pennsylvania (19 EVs), Harris could not reach 270 with Michigan and Wisconsin plus only Georgia (16), only North Carolina (16), or only Arizona+Nevada (17), which leaves her at 268-270. If she wins PA but loses MI (15), AZ+NV or GA alone works, but AZ alone does not.
evidence: EV arithmetic with 270toWin maps (267-271, 266-272).
forecasting_implication: Pennsylvania was the tipping-point state; narrow-path maps produce a median EV outcome near a tie even when the mean favors a candidate.

title: Oops! I made the convention bounce adjustment disappear.
insight: Biden's pre-debate path to exactly 270 via the Blue Wall states was fragile: losing any of PA, MI or WI, or even NH, would have cost him the election.
forecasting_implication: Maps that only just clear 270 are vulnerable to any single correlated miss.

title: Oops! I made the convention bounce adjustment disappear.
insight: Candidates with negligible convention bounces (Romney 2012, Kerry 2004, McGovern 1972, arguably Humphrey 1968) all lost.
evidence: Historical bounce table, 1964-2020.
forecasting_implication: Supports a symmetric bounce adjustment that penalizes the absence of a bounce.

title: Oops! I made the convention bounce adjustment disappear.
insight: The 2020 bounces (Biden 0, Trump +1) may have been limited by the mostly virtual COVID conventions.
forecasting_implication: Consider excluding 2020 when estimating typical bounce size.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
insight: Democrats generally have higher civic engagement, which makes debate-watcher audiences and instapolls lean Democratic.
evidence: Since 2000, the only Republicans to win the CNN instapoll were Romney in 2012 and Trump against Biden in 2024.
forecasting_implication: Discount instapolls for their Democratic lean.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
insight: After the 2024 DNC, swing-state polls were mediocre for Harris relative to national polls, suggesting a widening Electoral College-popular vote gap.
evidence: Model estimate of about 2.5 points of bias against Democrats.
forecasting_implication: Model the state-national gap explicitly rather than assuming the national margin translates directly.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
insight: Campaigns can be caught off guard when the news cycle moves on, for example Harris after the DNC.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
insight: With few undecided voters left, event-driven bounces are shrinking.
evidence: 95.4% of voters committed to Harris or Trump; debate bounces fell from about 4 points (Romney 2012) to about 2 points (Trump June 2024).
forecasting_implication: Expect smaller event effects in polarized elections.

title: Mad about the Electoral College? Blame California.
insight: The Democratic Electoral College disadvantage comes mainly from surplus votes in large, lopsided states (California, New York), not from the small-state bonus of two Senate-based electors per state.
evidence: House-based electors outnumber Senate-based electors more than 4:1 and are apportioned by population. California alone produced 3.6M excess Biden votes.
forecasting_implication: Model the popular vote–EC gap through state-level margin distributions. The gap moves with shifts in California and New York margins.

title: Mad about the Electoral College? Blame California.
insight: Texas and Florida, at mid-single-digit Trump margins, are close to an optimal vote distribution for Republicans: they are safely won without generating many wasted votes. If Florida became either more competitive or less competitive, Harris would be better off.
evidence: Projected Trump margins in FL and TX are in the mid-single digits.
forecasting_implication: Large red states at moderate margins produce right-tail Democratic upside in blowout scenarios but rarely matter in close races.

title: Mad about the Electoral College? Blame California.
insight: Parties pour resources into states within about 3 to 5 points of the tipping-point state. Bigger states attract investment at wider margins because of their larger reward.
evidence: Silver's empirical observation, also the basis of the NXV threshold.

title: Mad about the Electoral College? Blame California.
insight: California and New York are shifting toward Republicans. Democrats are losing ground with working-class Black, Hispanic and Asian American voters, and Silicon Valley and Wall Street communities have shifted right. The shift slightly reduces the EC/popular vote bias.
evidence: Projected margins: New York D+17 vs. Biden's 23, California D+25 vs. 29. Republicans had a strong 2022 midterm in New York.
forecasting_implication: Expect a somewhat smaller EC–popular vote gap than in 2020.

title: Mad about the Electoral College? Blame California.
insight: In 2020 Trump won more raw votes in California (6.0M) than in Texas (5.9M) or Florida (5.7M). New York was his fifth-highest state by raw votes.
evidence: 2020 results

title: Mad about the Electoral College? Blame California.
insight: Wisconsin was the 2020 tipping-point state, with Biden winning it by 0.7 points against 4.5 points nationally.
forecasting_implication: The roughly 3.8-point EC bias in 2020 is a benchmark for the popular vote–EC gap.

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
insight: Silver suggests the Biden-Trump race might not have been close. Replacing Biden with Harris made the race likely to be close.
evidence: Opinion; links to earlier analysis.
forecasting_implication: Candidate replacement can materially change competitiveness.

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
insight: Third-party candidates played little role in the 2024 Harris-Trump race, making it effectively two-way.
forecasting_implication: Error on the margin is about double the error on one candidate's share.

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
insight: Polls substantially underestimated Trump in both 2016 and 2020.
forecasting_implication: Allow for correlated systematic error across states.

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
insight: Recent US presidential elections can take several days to resolve after Election Day.
evidence: Recent elections
forecasting_implication: Communicate election-night uncertainty.

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
insight: Public emotional intensity about forecasts is much lower for midterms than for presidential elections.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
insight: Silver calls 2024 the closest election in his 16 years of forecasting, with all seven swing-state polling averages within 2 points.
evidence: State polling averages are all within 2 points.
forecasting_implication: Small systematic errors determine the outcome, so correlated error modeling matters most.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
insight: Michigan has been to the left of Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Since 2000 it voted Democratic by an average of 6.2 points, versus 3.8 for Pennsylvania and 3.5 for Wisconsin.
evidence: Average Democratic margins since 2000.
forecasting_implication: Use for state partisan-lean priors.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
insight: Arab Americans are only about 2% of Michigan's electorate, and Gaza is not necessarily a voting issue for swing voters. Harris has partially defused the issue relative to Biden.
evidence: About 2 percent of the electorate.
forecasting_implication: There is limited case for a special Michigan adjustment.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
insight: Pennsylvania is more likely to vote slightly Republican relative to the country, as it did in the prior two elections. It is the most likely tipping point largely because of its 19 electoral votes.
evidence: 2016 and 2020 results.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
insight: Polls underestimated Trump massively in Wisconsin in 2016 and 2020 but were accurate in 2022. Being whiter and more rural, Wisconsin is the frontline for any Trump overperformance with the white working class.
evidence: Past polling errors.
forecasting_implication: Wisconsin errors should be correlated with white working-class demographic error.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
insight: Nevada is in principle hard to poll because of a transient population that works irregular hours. In practice polls have mostly been accurate, except for underestimating Harry Reid in 2010, with Democrats typically outperforming polls by 1–2 points. Low turnout may make ground game matter. Working-class voters of color, especially in the casino industry, have shifted toward Trump in polls.
evidence: Historical poll accuracy.
forecasting_implication: Possible slight Democratic poll-miss tendency in Nevada.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
insight: North Carolina and Georgia are similar but not identical. North Carolina is whiter and was more Democratic-leaning than Georgia before 2020.
forecasting_implication: The two states are highly but imperfectly correlated.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
insight: Georgia polls have been highly accurate historically. No 2024 poll as of Sept 21 showed Harris ahead by 3 or more points. Georgia nearly was the tipping point in 2020, and a Georgia Election Board hand-count rule could make for a messy outcome.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
insight: Florida is a 'half' swing state. Harris had led no poll there all cycle, but its 30 electoral votes would effectively end Trump's chances if she won it. It is split into almost a dozen media markets, which makes it expensive to contest.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
insight: Without Texas's 40 electoral votes the GOP's Electoral College advantage collapses. Republicans have held Texas through a shift toward Trump among South Texas Hispanics, even as Dallas, Houston and Austin trend bluer.
forecasting_implication: Texas is a 1% tipping-point state.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
insight: New Hampshire is safe-ish for Harris: she has strong polling leads, the state is highly college-educated, and Biden won it easily in 2020. However, losing its 4 electoral votes would break the Blue Wall path.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
insight: There was a late Republican push to make Nebraska winner-take-all, which would eliminate NE-2's single electoral vote. Silver judged it unlikely to succeed and probably too late for Maine to reciprocate.
forecasting_implication: Electoral rules can change mid-cycle, so the model should handle district electoral votes flexibly.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
insight: Silver argues Harris should have picked Josh Shapiro because of Pennsylvania's pivotal role, though he notes home-state effects are small.

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
insight: 2024 polls showed signs of racial depolarization: white voters trending more Democratic and racial and ethnic minorities trending more Republican. This could produce more realignment than usual, with states like NH and FL moving off the map and Alaska coming into play.
evidence: Many polls this cycle; Selzer Iowa poll showing Harris down only 4 is consistent with this.
forecasting_implication: Historical state correlations may understate divergence between heavily Hispanic Sunbelt states and white Rust Belt states, so priors should let polls reveal the shift.

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
insight: Urban, white, well-educated districts such as NE-2 and KS-3 have been strong for Democrats.
evidence: KS-3 2022 result; NE-2 included in Harris's minimum path.

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
insight: The 2022 red-wave expectation was driven by vibes rather than data, and high-quality polls contradicted it.
evidence: NYT/Siena House district polls.
forecasting_implication: Weight objective polling data over narrative.

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
insight: A late 2024 Republican effort to make Nebraska winner-take-all appeared to have failed, so NE-2's electoral vote remained separately winnable.
forecasting_implication: Model NE-2 as a separate contest.

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
insight: The Electoral College penalty for Democrats was nearly 3 points in 2016 (PA tipping point) and nearly 4 points in 2020 (WI tipping point), and appears smaller in 2024.
evidence: 2016 D+2.1 national vs R+0.8 tipping point; 2020 D+4.5 vs D+0.6.
forecasting_implication: Don't assume a fixed Electoral College bias; let the state polls determine it.

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
insight: In 2020 Pennsylvania leaned GOP relative to the nation by about 3 points: Biden won PA by 1.2 and the nation by 4.5. A repeat gap would mean Harris losing PA by roughly 50,000 votes.
evidence: 2020 results

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
insight: Democratic deterioration in deep-blue states like New York shaves wasted votes and reduces the Electoral College gap without costing Democrats those states.
forecasting_implication: Bottom-up state modeling captures the effect of wasted votes on the popular vote/EC gap.

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
insight: In 2022 polls were not systematically biased against Democrats overall, but Democrats tended to slightly beat their polls in the closest state and district contests.
forecasting_implication: Possible swing-state turnout effects not captured by the model.

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
insight: Democrats have won the popular vote by at least 1.5 points in each of the past four elections.

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
insight: Arab American voters in Michigan swinging toward Trump over Gaza is a state-specific risk to Harris.
forecasting_implication: Illustrates idiosyncratic state-level error.

title: Which polls are biased toward Harris or Trump?
insight: In late September 2024, top-rated pollsters disagreed among themselves rather than diverging as a group from lower-rated ones. NYT/Siena had some bad data for Harris, while Selzer showed Harris down only 4 in Iowa.
evidence: Selzer Iowa poll: Harris down 4.
forecasting_implication: Quality-only averages would not change the picture much in 2024.

title: The 128 paths to the White House
insight: Harris polls slightly better with white voters than Biden's 2020 result but worse with Black, Hispanic and Asian American voters. This produces Rust Belt strength and Sun Belt weakness.
evidence: Polls show Trump narrowly ahead in GA while Harris expands margins in WI and NE-2.
forecasting_implication: State error correlations should be structured by demographic composition.

title: The 128 paths to the White House
insight: Some years, such as 2022, show little overall polling bias but large regional fluctuations that can partially offset each other.
evidence: 2022 example; AtlasIntel polls showing NC and NV as Harris's best states.
forecasting_implication: Model regional error components in addition to the national one.

title: The 128 paths to the White House
insight: 2020 had an EC/popular vote gap of nearly 4 points, so Biden needed close to his 4.5-point popular vote win. In 2024, a wide Rust Belt/Sun Belt gap could let Harris win with a popular vote lead as small as 0.5 points.
evidence: In 2020, five swing states were decided by under 1.5 points.
forecasting_implication: The EC-popular vote gap is variable and depends on the regional error pattern.

title: The 128 paths to the White House
insight: Nevada is distinctly bluer than the other Sun Belt states both historically and in recent polling. Michigan has the highest Black voter share of the Blue Wall states.

title: The 128 paths to the White House
insight: Polls held steady in the three weeks after the debate, unlike the slow deterioration for Harris that followed the DNC.

title: SBSQ #13: October Surprise edition
insight: The empirical literature on natural disasters and elections is mixed. One paper finds earthquakes help incumbents in affected cities. Another, on Hurricane Sandy in 2012, finds increased polarization: blue counties got bluer and red counties got redder.
evidence: Cited papers, not named in the text.
forecasting_implication: There is no clear directional adjustment for disasters; treat them as added uncertainty.

title: SBSQ #13: October Surprise edition
insight: Silver speculates that effective disaster recovery reminds voters of government's positive role, which should help the left. Hurricanes also raise the salience of climate change, a good issue for Democrats, and can let incumbents look presidential, though that is muddied with Biden not running.
evidence: Reasoning only.

title: SBSQ #13: October Surprise edition
insight: Hurricane Helene damage could lower turnout in predominantly red areas of North Carolina and Georgia. However, officials are making special efforts to protect voting, and voters sometimes defiantly overcome barriers; turnout was very high during COVID in 2020.
evidence: COVID 2020 turnout; North Carolina early voting accommodations.
forecasting_implication: Do not assume a large turnout penalty from disaster disruption.

title: SBSQ #13: October Surprise edition
insight: Silver judged escalating Middle East warfare and the port strike, which could significantly disrupt the economy, more likely than Helene to affect the 2024 campaign.

title: SBSQ #13: October Surprise edition
insight: Republican trust in mass media fell to 11% by 2023, versus 58% for Democrats and 29% for Independents, per Gallup. The decline is plausibly a linear trend driven by education polarization, with discontinuities around Fox News's rise in 2000 and the early Bush years and around Trump's emergence in 2016.
evidence: Gallup chart, 1972-2023. Republican trust was 68% in 1972, roughly 52% in 1998, and dropped to the teens after 2016.
forecasting_implication: This supports the view that the education realignment is shaping partisan coalitions.

title: 55/45 is a really close race
insight: In 2024, Democrats needed roughly a 2.5-point national popular-vote lead to be favored in the Electoral College. A Harris popular-vote win of 0-1 points gave her only about a 9.5% chance.
evidence: Oct 7, 2024 conditional probability table
forecasting_implication: Model the popular vote and the EC separately. The EC gap is sizeable and asymmetric.

title: 55/45 is a really close race
insight: Harris won the Sept 2024 debate and reestablished a consistent lead of about 3 points in national polls.
evidence: Forecast chart shift after the Sept 10 debate
forecasting_implication: Debates can arrest a trend.

title: 55/45 is a really close race
insight: RFK Jr.'s exit raised both major candidates' vote shares.
evidence: Popular vote chart
forecasting_implication: Reallocate a dropping-out third-party candidate's support to both major candidates, not just one.

title: 55/45 is a really close race
insight: In 2024, very few voters were undecided: the major candidates combined for 95.5% and third parties typically get 1-2%. This limits late movement.
evidence: National average
forecasting_implication: Late-race volatility should be lower when the undecided share is small.

title: When you should panic about the polls
insight: In 2016, 13% of voters decided in the final week and broke toward Trump (45-42) relative to earlier deciders, who favored Clinton 49-46. This was possibly enough to tip the Electoral College.
evidence: 2016 exit poll table: last week 13% (Clinton 42, Trump 45, other 13); before that 85% (Clinton 49, Trump 46, other 5).
forecasting_implication: Late shifts matter most when undecideds are numerous; justifies extra late-race responsiveness.

title: When you should panic about the polls
insight: 2016 had an unusually high number of undecided voters, which made Clinton more vulnerable than observers assumed.
forecasting_implication: Uncertainty should scale with the undecided share.

title: When you should panic about the polls
insight: Late deciders are in secular decline because people are constantly attuned to the news and early voting is increasing. Early voters are mostly strong partisans rather than swing voters.
forecasting_implication: The late-race volatility adjustment may matter less in recent cycles.

title: When you should panic about the polls
insight: Extreme partisanship and few undecideds make recent polling mostly stable, and news events rarely move numbers much.
evidence: Trump conviction moved polls about 0.5 points.
forecasting_implication: Expect small event effects; treat a 2-point weekly move as steep.

title: When you should panic about the polls
topic: media and partisan bias in reading polls
insight: Democrats are perpetually anxious and Republicans boastful about polls. Post-2016 media incentives lean toward portraying Republican prospects favorably, e.g., the unjustified 2022 'red wave' predictions, when polls and models showed an above-average Democratic midterm.
evidence: 2022 midterm example.
forecasting_implication: Discount narrative-driven expectations relative to polls and models.

title: When you should panic about the polls
insight: McCain polled strongly after the 2008 Republican convention, yet Obama won in a landslide.
forecasting_implication: Convention bounces are temporary and should be discounted.

title: When you should panic about the polls
insight: Winning the final news cycle probably helps, and late movement can sometimes be telling.

title: Why you should mostly ignore "internal polls"
insight: State-level shifts tend to move together uniformly, so the relative ordering of swing states stays stable even as the national margin swings by 7 points.
evidence: Tipping-point ordering was nearly unchanged between Trump +4 and Harris +3 nationally in 2024.
forecasting_implication: Model state outcomes as national swing plus a stable relative lean, with strong inter-state correlation.

title: Why you should mostly ignore "internal polls"
insight: Pennsylvania was the clear #1 tipping-point state in 2024. Michigan, Wisconsin, Georgia and North Carolina came next in some order, with Arizona and Nevada slightly behind.
evidence: Silver Bulletin tipping-point rankings.

title: Why you should mostly ignore "internal polls"
insight: Democrats tend to feel angsty and tolerate more public internal dissent than Trumpworld. Reports of Democratic panic therefore carry little signal.
forecasting_implication: Discount campaign-mood narratives.

title: Why you should mostly ignore "internal polls"
insight: Insider conventional wisdom has detached from reality before: the 2022 red wave narrative, and the 2016 belief that Clinton couldn't lose.
forecasting_implication: Do not adjust models toward insider narratives.

title: Why you should mostly ignore "internal polls"
insight: Harris gained for roughly 10 days after the Sept. 10 debate, then plateaued at a position not quite enough to lead in the Electoral College.
evidence: PA average Harris 48.6 vs Trump 47.6 on Oct 10.

title: New York Times polls are betting on a political realignment
insight: Red states have become redder and blue states bluer, producing many more landslide states.
evidence: 7 states decided by 20+ points in 1996 vs 19 in 2020.
forecasting_implication: Many states are non-competitive, and wasted votes affect the popular-vote/Electoral College relationship.

title: New York Times polls are betting on a political realignment
insight: Educational polarization among white voters grew from essentially none around 2006 to a large gap by 2020.
evidence: Biden won 54% of white college graduates vs 37% of white non-graduates (Catalist).
forecasting_implication: Education is a key demographic covariate for state lean and state correlation.

title: New York Times polls are betting on a political realignment
insight: Rising educational polarization implies Democratic erosion among working-class Black and Hispanic voters but gains among white voters. Because white voters are overrepresented in Electoral College impact, this trade could help Democrats in the Electoral College.
evidence: NYT/Siena showed Trump at 15% of Black voters vs 9% in 2020. NBC/Telemundo showed Harris +14 among Hispanics vs Biden +26-28 in 2020.
forecasting_implication: This could make a Harris popular-vote loss with an Electoral College win plausible. Correlated demographic shifts should affect state correlations.

title: New York Times polls are betting on a political realignment
topic: Rust Belt vs Sun Belt divergence
insight: If the realignment is real, Harris should gain in whiter Blue Wall states (MI, WI, PA) and Trump in the diverse Sun Belt. If minority shifts toward Trump occur without offsetting white gains, the result is a Trump landslide.
evidence: NYT/Siena PA Harris +4 vs AZ Trump +6.
forecasting_implication: There is a scenario dimension in which Sun Belt and Rust Belt states decouple.

title: New York Times polls are betting on a political realignment
insight: 2024 polls show Harris underperforming Biden in deep-blue states (including fairly white Massachusetts), so the pattern is not cleanly racial.
evidence: Regression white-share coefficient p=0.261.
forecasting_implication: Do not over-engineer a racial swing term; the evidence is weak.

title: New York Times polls are betting on a political realignment
insight: Recent elections have been extremely similar from one to the next, so betting on persistence has usually worked.
evidence: Uniform 2.4-point swing from 2016 reproduces 2020.
forecasting_implication: Strong prior on the previous-election state map plus a uniform national swing.

title: New York Times polls are betting on a political realignment
insight: Voters of the minority party in lopsided states, such as Massachusetts Republicans, have little reason to turn out. This could make results more polarized than polls show.
forecasting_implication: Possible state-lean-dependent polling bias.

title: Are Republican pollsters “flooding the zone?”
insight: In October 2024, Republican-aligned pollsters were modestly more favorable to Trump than other firms, about 1.4 points on the margin, rather than dramatically so.
evidence: Flat averages of October national polls: D+2.0 for Republican-aligned firms vs D+3.4 for non-Republican-aligned firms.
forecasting_implication: House effect adjustment and quality weighting are sufficient to neutralize partisan firms. Excluding them yields small shifts of about 0.4 points.

title: Are Republican pollsters “flooding the zone?”
insight: Mid-October tightening toward Trump may reflect the tail end of Harris's post-debate bounce, random noise, or the start of a Trump surge.
evidence: Trump gained 0.3 points nationally in a week, and about 0.7-1.1 points in PA, MI and WI.
forecasting_implication: Avoid overreacting to small weekly moves.

title: Does Trump have momentum?
insight: Bandwagon and momentum effects are overrated in two-way general elections because media sentiment shifts rapidly. A 'candidate rising' storyline becomes stale after about two weeks, and the media then looks for a comeback narrative.
evidence: Silver's experience as a model builder and observer of news cycles.
forecasting_implication: Do not extrapolate trends in general-election polling averages; treat them as close to a random walk.

title: Does Trump have momentum?
insight: Momentum effects can matter a great deal in multi-candidate primaries where voters behave tactically.
evidence: In 2020, as Elizabeth Warren slumped in the polls, many of her voters switched to Bernie Sanders as the more viable progressive alternative to Joe Biden.
forecasting_implication: Primary models may need dynamics that allow trends to continue, unlike general-election models.

title: Does Trump have momentum?
insight: Republicans more actively cultivate momentum narratives and develop a pack mentality after strong Trump polls, while Democrats tend to fear that leads will evaporate.
forecasting_implication: Expect prediction markets and partisan commentary to overreact to pro-Trump trends.

title: Does Trump have momentum?
insight: In 2024, the Blue Wall states (MI, WI, PA) dominated Harris's path to victory. North Carolina could substitute for Michigan or Wisconsin on its own, but substituting for Pennsylvania would also require winning Nevada.
evidence: 61% combined tipping-point probability for the Blue Wall states; footnote 3.
forecasting_implication: Model state correlation regionally; Blue Wall states tend to move together.

title: Does Trump have momentum?
insight: Harris remained a clear but not overwhelming favorite in the popular vote while being roughly 50/50 in the Electoral College, which reflects a Republican Electoral College bias.
forecasting_implication: Simulate the Electoral College gap separately from the popular vote.

title: Likability isn't enough
insight: Likability does not equal vote share. Voters may support a disliked candidate they see as fighting for them on clear policy goals ('Billboard Lawyer' effect).
evidence: Harris led Trump on favorability by 3.2 to 5.2 points but led national polls by only 1.6 points. Clinton showed a similar pattern in 2016.
forecasting_implication: Do not use the favorability gap as a predictor of late movement toward the more-liked candidate.

title: Likability isn't enough
insight: 'Democracy' messaging resonates with Democrats' college-educated base but not particularly with swing voters.
evidence: Silver cites polling (linked).

title: Likability isn't enough
insight: Abortion is a good issue for Democrats.
evidence: Linked reference.

title: Likability isn't enough
insight: Recent incumbent-party campaigns have mostly failed amid persistent voter dissatisfaction with the country's direction: McCain in 2008, Clinton in 2016, Trump in 2020, and Biden effectively in 2024. Obama in 2012 was the exception.
evidence: Election history 2008-2024.
forecasting_implication: Supports a headwind for the incumbent party in an environment of anti-incumbent sentiment and unpopular incumbents.

title: Likability isn't enough
insight: After Harris replaced Biden, the race was near 50/50 for most of the campaign. Harris succeeded in the set pieces (consolidating Democrats, the convention, the debate), then the race drifted slightly toward Trump. Heavy early voting limits late strategy changes.

title: Likability isn't enough
insight: Silver faults Harris for choosing Walz over Josh Shapiro, citing partly Electoral College (Pennsylvania) implications and partly the lost signal of a pivot to the center.
forecasting_implication: Implies a possible home-state VP effect, though this is not quantified.

title: Likability isn't enough
insight: The US public is still generally more sympathetic to Israel than to Palestine.
evidence: Linked polling.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
insight: Democrats are more likely to respond to political surveys, which caused Trump to beat his polls in 2016 and by a wider margin in 2020.
evidence: Trump beat polls in 2016 and 2020; there is little evidence for the shy-voter theory.
forecasting_implication: Watch pollster weighting choices, such as past vote and partisanship, rather than modeling 'shy' voters.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
insight: There is no persistent worldwide tendency for right-wing parties to outperform their polls. Le Pen's National Rally underperformed its polls in the 2024 French legislative elections.
evidence: French 2024 legislative elections; UK 2017 Labour overperformance.
forecasting_implication: Do not apply a systematic right-wing bias correction.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
insight: As of October 2024, Georgia and Arizona tilted toward Trump while MI, NC, NV, PA and WI were basically toss-ups.
evidence: Silver Bulletin forecast, October 22, 2024.
forecasting_implication: Sweep probabilities are asymmetric when leads are asymmetric, even under unbiased error.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
insight: Some UK pollsters made ad hoc adjustments for 'shy Tories', and Labour beat its polls as Conservatives lost their majority.
forecasting_implication: Pollster overcorrection is a real risk after high-profile misses.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
insight: Republicans were once the higher-propensity party and did better in low-turnout elections. Democrats now dominate among educated suburban voters and excel in low-turnout environments like special elections, while Trump relies on irregular voters who turn out mainly in presidential years.
evidence: Historical LV boosts for the GOP, e.g. 2004; recent special election performance.
forecasting_implication: Do not assume LV screens or low turnout favor Republicans. The direction of the LV adjustment should be estimated empirically each cycle.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
insight: LV screens helping Trump in swing states but Harris nationally is puzzling, since swing states like NC and PA demographically resemble the nation. Possible explanations include campaign intensity, ads, Trump's closing message or ground game in swing states, or pollster methodology.
evidence: State LV shift of R+0.5 vs national LV shift of D+0.5.
forecasting_implication: The Electoral College gap estimate may be sensitive to LV methodology. If Trump outperforms the polls, national polls may have missed an enthusiasm advantage.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
insight: Democrats have lost their longstanding edge in party identification, so turning out their base is no longer enough. Harris probably needs to win independents or crossover voters.
evidence: In Nevada, the Democratic active-registration advantage fell from 87,000 in November 2020 to about 20,000.
forecasting_implication: Do not infer vote share from party-registration turnout. Shifts in registration are already priced into polls.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
insight: Harris likely needs to win the popular vote by some margin to win the Electoral College.
forecasting_implication: The model should allow for a popular vote/Electoral College gap that favors Republicans.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
insight: The shift in registration toward Republicans has been underway for several years, yet Democrats had a relatively strong 2022 midterm in the swing states. Possible causes: young first-time registrants turned off by older Democratic candidates, and no competitive Democratic primary in 2024.
evidence: 2022 midterm results
forecasting_implication: Registration trends are weak predictors of results.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
insight: West Virginia has many registered Democrats who vote Republican, and Colorado is ancestrally Republican but votes Democratic. Registration lags behind actual partisanship.
evidence: West Virginia: D+12 in the early vote vs. Trump +41.7 in 2016
forecasting_implication: Adjust registration-based data for ancestral party registration.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
insight: There are few crossover voters in partisan times. The overwhelming majority of registered Democrats and Republicans vote for their party's nominee.
evidence: In October 2024 polls, Harris wins 6% of Republicans and Trump wins 3.5% of Democrats.

title: There’s more herding in swing state polls than at a sheep farm in the Scottish Highlands
insight: Pennsylvania was the most likely tipping-point state in 2024, so polling there is tantamount to weighing in on the Electoral College.
forecasting_implication: Herding pressure is greatest in the highest-stakes states.

title: There’s more herding in swing state polls than at a sheep farm in the Scottish Highlands
insight: 2024 crosstabs showed sharp moves away from Democrats among Black and Hispanic voters and some gains among white voters. If real, they imply a scrambled map with Georgia tougher for Harris, which most toplines did not reflect.
evidence: NYT/Siena: Harris strong in PA but weak in AZ/GA.
forecasting_implication: Allow for state errors in opposite directions driven by demographic composition.

title: There’s more herding in swing state polls than at a sheep farm in the Scottish Highlands
insight: Strong Harris numbers in Iowa (Selzer), Kansas, and NE-02 would imply comfortable wins in demographically similar states like Michigan and Wisconsin.
forecasting_implication: Use correlated demographic structure to read low-attention state polls as signals for swing states.

title: There’s more herding in swing state polls than at a sheep farm in the Scottish Highlands
insight: Wisconsin has had major polling errors in the past, and its pollsters appear especially reluctant to go out on a limb. It showed the most herding (92% of polls within 2.5 points).
evidence: 33 of 36 polls close
forecasting_implication: Be skeptical of tight clustering in Wisconsin polls.

title: A shocking Iowa poll means somebody is going to be wrong
insight: Iowa trended strongly red through 2020 (Trump +8). Selzer polls in 2024 swung from Trump +18 versus Biden in June to Trump +4 versus Harris in September to Harris +3 in November.
evidence: Selzer/Des Moines Register polls
forecasting_implication: Large candidate-switch effects are possible. Treat single-pollster series in sparse states carefully.

title: A shocking Iowa poll means somebody is going to be wrong
insight: Harris held up in the Midwest (except Minnesota), NE-02 and Ohio, and lost ground in Florida, the Southwest (NV, AZ), New York and Virginia, which may be tied to state-level inflation.
evidence: NE-02 average Harris +9.6 vs Biden's 6.6 in 2020; Ohio poll Harris -3; a tight Kansas poll; inflation regression
forecasting_implication: Regional, not uniform, swing structure; consider state-level economic conditions.

title: A shocking Iowa poll means somebody is going to be wrong
insight: Crosstabs show Harris losing ground with Black and Latino voters, but toplines move little. These shifts may be real and even larger than published polls show.
forecasting_implication: Sun Belt states with large minority populations may carry correlated error.

title: A shocking Iowa poll means somebody is going to be wrong
insight: Harris had underwhelming margins in Minnesota despite Tim Walz being her running mate.
forecasting_implication: The VP home-state effect may be small.

title: The polls are close, but that doesn’t mean the results will be
insight: Polling errors are often regional. In 2016 the polls were fairly accurate in the West, while the big misses came east of the Mississippi, especially in the Upper Midwest.
evidence: A 2016 shift map from Obama 2012 to Clinton
forecasting_implication: Model correlated regional and demographic error terms, not only a uniform national swing.

title: The polls are close, but that doesn’t mean the results will be
insight: In the 2022 midterms, polls were biased toward Republicans in competitive races in Arizona and Pennsylvania but were slightly too favorable to Democrats overall.
forecasting_implication: State-level error can diverge in sign from the national error.

title: The polls are close, but that doesn’t mean the results will be
insight: In today's polarized environment, about 319 electoral votes from a sweep of the swing states is what passes for a landslide.

title: The polls are close, but that doesn’t mean the results will be
insight: The direction of polling misses has alternated: polls underestimated Obama in 2012 and Trump in 2016 and 2020.
forecasting_implication: Do not build in a directional bias based on recent cycles.

title: A random number generator determined the “favorite" in our forecast
insight: Black and Hispanic voters were considerably more likely than white voters to be undecided late in 2024, which could favor Harris if they 'come home'. In the NYT/Siena October poll, 7% of nonwhite voters were undecided versus 4% of white voters, and 6% of independents versus 2% of partisans. Young voters (18-29) were most often 'probable, not definite' at 25%.
evidence: NYT/Siena October national likely voter poll table.
forecasting_implication: Allocation of undecideds by demographic group can shift late projections.

title: A random number generator determined the “favorite" in our forecast
insight: There was evidence of a late Harris rebound with Latino voters, including a Univision poll of Pennsylvania Latinos showing Harris up 64-30. This was better than her earlier crosstabs and better than Biden in 2020, possibly helped by the Madison Square Garden 'Puerto Rico' remark.
evidence: Univision poll; Pennsylvania's large Puerto Rican population.
forecasting_implication: Single-group polls may signal late shifts not captured in topline averages.

title: A random number generator determined the “favorite" in our forecast
insight: Worldwide there is an anti-incumbent mood and a conservative shift, especially on immigration, which favors Trump.

title: A random number generator determined the “favorite" in our forecast
insight: The 'incumbent rule' is ambiguous in 2024: Trump was a former president, while Harris was the incumbent vice president.
forecasting_implication: Incumbency variables need care when candidates do not fit standard categories.

title: A random number generator determined the “favorite" in our forecast
insight: Abortion referendums in Nevada and Arizona and Mark Robinson's candidacy in North Carolina may help Harris.

title: A random number generator determined the “favorite" in our forecast
insight: Slightly more Democrats than Republicans voted early in party-registration states, with margins down from 2020. Silver says 2020 is a poor comparison because of COVID.
forecasting_implication: Early vote comparisons to 2020 are confounded.

title: A random number generator determined the “favorite" in our forecast
insight: Fundraising may now be underweighted after an overcorrection, though top-of-ticket candidates have more money than they need. Harris led strongly on fundraising.

title: FINAL Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential election forecast
insight: In 2024 the Electoral College was expected to favor Republicans by roughly 2-3 points. Harris needed about a D+2.5 popular-vote margin to be a slight favorite.
evidence: Harris won 14.3% of simulations at D+0-1, 32.5% at D+1-2 and 58.2% at D+2-3. Harris winning the popular vote but losing the Electoral College had a 26% chance.
forecasting_implication: Model state outcomes relative to the national vote rather than assuming the popular-vote winner takes the Electoral College.

title: FINAL Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential election forecast
insight: A 269-269 tie would likely be decided for Trump in the House, which votes by state delegation.
evidence: Author's statement.
forecasting_implication: Allocate tie outcomes to the party with more House state delegations when computing effective win probability.

title: FINAL Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential election forecast
insight: In a polarized climate, most presidential elections are close and candidates are rarely out of the running.
forecasting_implication: Avoid overconfidence; keep meaningful tail probabilities.

title: FINAL Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential election forecast
insight: The seven 2024 swing states tend to move together, so sweeps by either side are the likeliest outcomes.
forecasting_implication: Use strongly correlated state errors in simulation.

title: The model exactly predicted the most likely election map
topic: blue-state erosion and Electoral College bias
insight: Harris underperformed most in deep-blue states (CA, NJ, IL, HI, NY especially NYC, MD). Those were wasted votes for Democrats, so losing them, combined with Republicans gaining surplus votes in FL and TX, could greatly reduce or even reverse the Electoral College bias.
evidence: Conditional deltas of roughly +4 to +8 for Trump in these states; Trump lost NJ by only about 5.
forecasting_implication: Expect a smaller Republican Electoral College advantage relative to the popular vote in future cycles; update state partisan leans accordingly.

title: The model exactly predicted the most likely election map
insight: Conservatives leaving high-cost blue states move to Florida and Texas, making those states redder. Liberal emigres move to Washington, Oregon, Colorado and to some extent Maine, making those states bluer.
evidence: FL +4.1, TX +2.9; WA −4.7, OR −4.4, CO −2.8 conditional deltas.
forecasting_implication: Uniform swing from the previous election misses migration-driven trends; consider trend terms for partisan lean.

title: The model exactly predicted the most likely election map
insight: Utah is gradually becoming more purple because of a tech workforce and Mormon coolness toward Trump. It will not be a swing state by 2028 but possibly by 2040.
evidence: Trump −6.9 vs projection

title: The model exactly predicted the most likely election map
insight: North Dakota has been getting redder amid the fracking boom.
evidence: +6.0 Trump overperformance

title: The model exactly predicted the most likely election map
insight: New Mexico remained solidly blue and often does not follow the trends of other heavily Hispanic states.
evidence: Trump −1.6 vs projection
forecasting_implication: Do not over-correlate New Mexico with other Hispanic-heavy states.

title: The model exactly predicted the most likely election map
insight: Harris's 2-point loss in Georgia, smaller than in other swing states, moves Georgia closer to the tipping point. Georgia may trend blue relative to the nation.
evidence: Georgia −1.9 vs projection

title: The model exactly predicted the most likely election map
insight: In 2024 Democrats mostly held Black voters, while Hispanic, Asian American and 'other' voters became true swing demographics.
evidence: Exit poll chart: White 41D/57R, Black 85/13, Hispanic 52/46, Asian 54/39, Other 42/54.
forecasting_implication: Demographic correlation structures should allow Hispanic and Asian vote shifts independent of Black voters.

title: The model exactly predicted the most likely election map
insight: Trump overperformance among northern whites links the Blue Wall states with Maine, New Hampshire and Minnesota. Nevada behaves differently from the Blue Wall states.
forecasting_implication: Model correlated regional and demographic blocs.

title: The model exactly predicted the most likely election map
insight: Delaware likely showed residual sympathy for Biden.
evidence: −3.3 delta
forecasting_implication: Home-state effects can carry over to a party's subsequent ticket.

title: The model exactly predicted the most likely election map
insight: Silver argues that Democrats' tendency to cast out people who disagree on hot-button issues (such as COVID school closures or Biden's age) hurts majority-building, while Trump welcomed all comers.
evidence: Anecdotal reactions to the newsletter's coverage

title: SBSQ #15: Democrats have a "fool me twice" problem
insight: Arab American voters in Dearborn cast a large protest vote against Harris over Israel policy, despite Trump being likely more hawkish.
evidence: Harris 36%, Trump 42%, Stein and others more than 20%; Harris as low as 13% in some precincts; Biden almost 70% in 2020.
forecasting_implication: Concentrated issue-driven groups can swing sharply and toward third parties.

title: SBSQ #15: Democrats have a "fool me twice" problem
insight: Silver argues that voters punish parties for broken promises or coercive 'the other side is worse' messaging, and that this is often near-rational as a deterrence strategy.
evidence: Biden's broken 'return to normalcy' promise; the 2021 approval collapse that never recovered; Zeldin coming within 6 points of Hochul in 2022.
forecasting_implication: Incumbent-party performance failures can outweigh relative policy preferences.

title: SBSQ #15: Democrats have a "fool me twice" problem
insight: Biden's approval turned south in summer 2021, amid the Delta variant, inflation and supply chain problems, and never recovered.

title: SBSQ #15: Democrats have a "fool me twice" problem
insight: Silver rates Trump a better candidate than previously credited, Clinton below average but above replacement level, and Biden highly context-dependent. He counts Biden's record as 1-1 since Biden lost the 2024 race before withdrawing.
evidence: Trump won after January 6 and 34 felony charges while gaining in Democratic groups; Clinton won the popular vote.
forecasting_implication: Candidate effects can be substantial and context-dependent.

title: SBSQ #15: Democrats have a "fool me twice" problem
insight: State ordering is somewhat persistent, so the small 2024 Electoral College bias against Democrats suggests little bias in 2028. However, Trump's coalition may not be durable, and anti-incumbent sentiment could favor Democrats.
evidence: The GOP lost the popular vote four times in a row before 2024; Trump's margin was narrower than any of those Democratic popular-vote wins.
forecasting_implication: Expect persistence in partisan lean ordering, but keep some uncertainty about coalition durability.

title: SBSQ #15: Democrats have a "fool me twice" problem
insight: Harris's smaller losses in swing states may reflect tactical voting incentives, not only campaign effectiveness. Voters in safe states can 'send a message' or abstain.
evidence: Harris lost all of the swing states and lost even more ground in noncompetitive states.
forecasting_implication: Swings may differ systematically between competitive and safe states.

title: SBSQ #15: Democrats have a "fool me twice" problem
insight: A persistent global anti-incumbent mood may advantage the out-party.
forecasting_implication: Supports incumbency penalty assumptions.

title: Polling is becoming more of an art than a science
insight: Pollsters disagree on whether Republican underestimation is Trump-specific or reflects broader partisan nonresponse among less-educated, low-propensity voters. Jackson leans Trump-specific, contingent on whether the 2028 nominee (e.g., Vance vs Haley) inherits his low-propensity coalition. Cohn and Ruffini see it as broader.
evidence: Underestimation in 2016/2020/2024 but not in 2018/2022. Ruffini cites growing evidence of Senate polls underestimating Republicans. Cohn cites 2000s surveys with too many college grads in unweighted data.
forecasting_implication: Uncertainty about the direction of systematic polling bias may need to differ when Trump is versus isn't on the ballot. 2026 Senate results will be a test.

title: Polling is becoming more of an art than a science
insight: Polls correctly detected movement toward the GOP among nonwhite and younger voters across recent cycles.
evidence: Ruffini's 2023 book and campaign experience.

title: Polling is becoming more of an art than a science
insight: Questions on the economy, immigration, and Biden's approval, plus Harris's inability to separate from the administration, were leading indicators of Trump's 2024 win.
evidence: Jackson's reading of 2024 polling data.
forecasting_implication: Supports using incumbent approval and economic sentiment as fundamentals for the incumbent party's successor candidate.

title: Polling is becoming more of an art than a science
insight: 2026 is a midterm in which Democrats are expected to fare well.
forecasting_implication: Consistent with a midterm penalty for the president's party.

title: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings 2024 archive
insight: Presidential primary polls are far less accurate than general election polls, missing the top-two margin by about 9-10 points on average.
evidence: 9.7 points in the 2024 GOP primaries; 9.3 points on average since 2000.
forecasting_implication: Primary forecasts need much wider uncertainty than general election forecasts.

title: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings 2024 archive
insight: 2024 GOP primary polls overstated Trump's margin over Haley.
evidence: 4.4 points on average.
forecasting_implication: Frontrunner margins in primary polls may be overstated.

title: So, how did the polls do in 2024? It’s complicated
insight: With less ticket-splitting in presidential years, polling bias is nearly identical across presidential, Senate and House races.
evidence: In 2024, bias was D+2.9 for president, Senate and House.
forecasting_implication: Model polling errors as highly correlated across offices within a presidential year.

title: So, how did the polls do in 2024? It’s complicated
insight: Polls underestimated Republicans when Trump was on the ballot (2016, 2020, 2024) but not in the 2018 and 2022 midterms.
evidence: 2018 bias R+0.5 and 2022 bias D+0.8 combined, versus D+3.0, D+4.7 and D+2.9 in presidential years.
forecasting_implication: Consider whether to apply a prior on directional bias in future cycles without Trump on the ballot; the evidence is uncertain.

title: So, how did the polls do in 2024? It’s complicated
insight: Trump's unpopularity is expected to carry electoral consequences for Republicans in 2025 special elections and the 2026 midterms.
forecasting_implication: Presidential approval feeds into midterm expectations.

title: So, how did the polls do in 2024? It’s complicated
insight: Pollsters concentrate resources on competitive states and rarely poll safe states such as Alabama or Vermont.
forecasting_implication: Safe states have sparse polling, so fundamentals or priors matter more there.

title: How low is Trump's popularity floor?
insight: Lame-duck presidents have lower average approval and lower floors than in their first terms. Partisans may throw a second-term president under the bus, though partisanship can inhibit this.
evidence: Average for re-elected presidents: 58.0 to 48.0; floor 47.1 to 37.7. Johnson, Nixon and Bush cratered.
forecasting_implication: Midterm environment priors for 2026 should allow more downside in a second-term president's approval than his first term suggests.

title: How low is Trump's popularity floor?
insight: Trump has a relatively high and stable approval floor because of polarization and a passionate base. The base case is a high floor.
evidence: First-term range 37.8 to 45.0, the narrowest ever.
forecasting_implication: Use narrower variance for Trump approval, but widen it for the second-term effect.

title: How low is Trump's popularity floor?
insight: Voters are grumpy toward all politicians. Democrats' numbers have also cratered, so Trump's decline does not automatically translate into Democratic gains in a hypothetical rematch.
evidence: Trump won the tipping-point state, Pennsylvania, by 1.7 points.
forecasting_implication: Do not map presidential disapproval one-to-one onto opposition-party support.

title: How low is Trump's popularity floor?
insight: Recent converts to Trump may defect first: young voters, Hispanic and Asian Americans, Black men, and 'Riverian' elites. Young voters are less partisan and more fickle.
evidence: Trump won or nearly won young voters in 2024, and minorities shifted heavily toward him.
forecasting_implication: Watch subgroup approval among recent converts as a leading indicator.

title: How low is Trump's popularity floor?
insight: Silver assumes racial depolarization may be robust: Democrats are holding white voters while losing minorities, especially younger ones. Lost loyalty is hard to regain.
evidence: The shift is concentrated among younger Black, Hispanic and Asian voters.
forecasting_implication: Do not assume reversion of the minority shift in 2026/2028 baselines.

title: How low is Trump's popularity floor?
insight: Trump could lose his white working-class base. Tariffs may hit manufacturing-dependent states especially hard. Voters may not forgive a tariff-induced recession the way they forgave the COVID recession. Trump's economic approval is worse than at any point in his first term.
forecasting_implication: Allow for regionally correlated swings in manufacturing states.

title: How low is Trump's popularity floor?
insight: All methods for breaking down election results by demographic group rely on statistical extrapolation or polling. There is no hard-and-fast way to know group vote shares.
evidence: Data sources disagree on whether Trump or Harris won young voters.
forecasting_implication: Treat subgroup vote estimates as uncertain inputs.

title: We're tracking more data on Trump's popularity
insight: Trump's issue pattern has reversed from his first term. The economy was his strongest issue then; in 2025 it is a considerably bigger liability, while immigration is among his least bad issues even though it has declined.
evidence: Issue averages as of May 2025: immigration -0.2, economy -13.5, trade -17.7, inflation -24.7.
forecasting_implication: The economy and inflation may now drive Republican midterm weakness.

title: We're tracking more data on Trump's popularity
insight: Strong disapproval exceeding strong approval suggests Trump's negatives are more entrenched than his positives, which is bearish for him. The same pattern held in his first term, especially its first two years, and preceded Democrats gaining 41 House seats in 2018.
evidence: Strong-view net approval -14.5 vs. overall -7.3; 2018 Democratic gain of 41 House seats.
forecasting_implication: Intensity gaps may signal a turnout advantage for the opposition in midterms.

title: We're tracking more data on Trump's popularity
insight: Democrats have consistently overperformed in special elections in recent years because of lopsided turnout in their favor. This gives an indirect read on the political environment but is skewed by turnout.
forecasting_implication: Discount special-election swings for turnout effects when estimating the national environment.

title: We're tracking more data on Trump's popularity
insight: Even if polls miss some Trump voters, it won't help Republicans in 2026 if those voters do not turn out when Trump is not on the ballot.
forecasting_implication: Don't automatically carry the presidential-year Republican polling bias into midterm forecasts.

title: We're tracking more data on Trump's popularity
insight: Some voters may be relatively sensitive to stock prices. Trump's slight rebound in approval coincided with a more conciliatory tone on tariffs and a stock-market rise.
evidence: Trade approval ticked up and economic approval stabilized in late April and early May 2025.

title: We're tracking more data on Trump's popularity
insight: Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp declining a Senate bid, and Republican fears of putting safe Trump seats in play, suggest Republicans themselves expect a rough 2026.
forecasting_implication: Candidate recruitment decisions can serve as qualitative signals of the national environment.

title: SBSQ #21: Why young men don't like Democrats
insight: Essentially all of Harris's decline relative to Biden came from men. The gender gap expanded, especially among young voters and Black and Latino men. Gen Z men voted majority Trump in 2024.
evidence: Catalist Figure 29, change in Democratic support 2020-2024 (women/men, percentage points): Total -1/-5; White +0/-4; Black -1/-8; Latino -7/-12; Asian -3/-6.
forecasting_implication: Demographic shifts in the 2024 coalition are concentrated among men, especially nonwhite and young men.

title: SBSQ #21: Why young men don't like Democrats
insight: Men are much more positive toward capitalism than women. Young people are less positive toward capitalism than older people.
evidence: Pew chart, positive impression of capitalism: men 68%, women 48%; ages 18-29 40%, 65+ 73%. Socialism: men 35%, women 38%; 18-29 44%. Census data: 61% of small businesses are majority-owned by men vs 22% by women. YouGov Musk favorability: men 48-46, women 34-58.
forecasting_implication: Anti-corporate messaging is unlikely to reduce the gender gap.

title: SBSQ #21: Why young men don't like Democrats
topic: economic optimism by gender and age
insight: Gen Z men were more optimistic about the economy than women and older cohorts in 2022.
evidence: CES 2022 share saying the economy was staying the same or getting better: Gen Z men 29%, Gen Z women 21% (the text says 22%), older men 26%, older women 22%. This came despite Biden being president, which would ordinarily depress men's optimism.

title: SBSQ #21: Why young men don't like Democrats
insight: Higher self-reported mental health is strongly correlated with conservative views. The gender gap in self-reported mental health is much larger for Gen Z.
evidence: CES 2022 (liberal/moderate/conservative): Excellent 20/30/51; Very good 26/35/39; Good 32/36/32; Fair 39/37/24; Poor 45/35/19. Silver says the pattern holds within subsamples. Chart readings: Gen Z men ~37% and Gen Z women ~21% report very good or excellent mental health, vs Silent generation men ~75% and women ~69%.

title: SBSQ #21: Why young men don't like Democrats
insight: Young liberal men, not conservatives, are more active posting about politics on social media.
evidence: CES 2022: among Gen Z men who posted about politics, Democrats outnumbered Republicans 42-22. Among those who didn't post, the split was 30-19, with a majority identifying as independent, other, or not sure.
forecasting_implication: Online political discourse is not representative of young men's partisanship.

title: SBSQ #21: Why young men don't like Democrats
topic: gender vs racial/immigration attitudes among young men
insight: Gen Z men show gender resentment similar to older men but much less anti-immigrant sentiment.
evidence: CES: share agreeing women are 'too easily offended': Gen Z men 40%, Gen Z women 20%, older men 41%, older women 32%. Share supporting a 50% cut in legal immigration: Gen Z men 30%, Gen Z women 22%, older men 49%, older women 44%.

title: SBSQ #21: Why young men don't like Democrats
insight: Trump fared better in 2024 among voters who consume little political news. Silver reads this as possibly winning the apolitical 'normie' vote rather than only uninformed voters.
forecasting_implication: Low-engagement voters lean Trump, which bears on turnout modeling and polls of engaged respondents.

title: SBSQ #21: Why young men don't like Democrats
insight: Men generally have higher risk tolerance than women, and younger people more than older people. Silver suggests this links to Democrats' weakness with young men.
evidence: Silver's research for On the Edge.

title: SBSQ #21: Why young men don't like Democrats
insight: The NYC Democratic primary electorate is more moderate than assumed. Many registered Democrats are de facto Republicans because Republicans rarely win citywide. The electorate is majority nonwhite, and nonwhite Democrats tend to be more moderate than white Democrats.
evidence: 65% of NYC voters are registered Democrats. Emerson poll: 13% of the Democratic primary electorate voted Trump and 15% view him favorably, about 3x the share among Democrats nationwide. Bernie Sanders's best 2016 states were the whitest. Trump gained in every borough in 2020 and 2024.
forecasting_implication: In primaries, the center-left candidate is often closer to the median voter.

title: SBSQ #21: Why young men don't like Democrats
insight: Turnout in NYC Democratic mayoral primaries is low, and turnout surges can reshape outcomes. Media attention from a tightening race could raise turnout and polarize voters around an insurgent.
evidence: Turnout ranged from 11-30% of registered Democrats in the past six mayoral primaries. Primaries moved from September to June starting in 2019.
forecasting_implication: Low and variable turnout increases primary forecast uncertainty.

title: SBSQ #21: Why young men don't like Democrats
insight: In ranked-choice primaries, an insurgent must avoid becoming so polarizing that other candidates' voters rank the frontrunner above him.
evidence: Mamdani vs Cuomo, 2025.
forecasting_implication: Final-round RCV polling depends on lower-ranked preferences, which can shift.

title: SBSQ #21: Why young men don't like Democrats
insight: A questioner claims the NYT endorsement lifted Kathryn Garcia from single digits to a close second in 2021.
evidence: Questioner claim, not verified by Silver.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
insight: Taking more popular, typically more central, positions helps candidates win. Silver treats this as a persistent background force that is sometimes outweighed but always present.
evidence: Theoretical, plus district-level WAR evidence and macro evidence.
forecasting_implication: Include candidate ideology or moderation as a predictor. Treat a null finding with skepticism.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
insight: In recent elections voters perceived the Democratic Party as having moved too far left, even compared with Trump, and this coincided with a rough electoral era for the party.
evidence: Survey perceptions (linked).

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
insight: More issues have collapsed onto a single left-right axis, making the MVT more relevant. At the same time preferences have grown bimodal (e.g., 45/10/45), which weakens the payoff from centrism.
evidence: Illustrative 45-10-45 distribution.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
insight: Partisanship increasingly swallows moderation, incumbency and experience effects. Candidate quality matters less than it used to.
evidence: Herschel Walker's narrow loss; Silver's 2022 model change.
forecasting_implication: Shrink candidate-quality coefficients in recent cycles.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
insight: As the parties become ideologically coherent, voters rationally infer more from the party label and assume even Hogan or Manchin types will do their leaders' bidding.
forecasting_implication: Expect smaller personal-vote effects for moderates in federal races.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
insight: Thermostatic backlash has grown stronger. Presidents struggle to stay popular, their ideas lose popularity once they are in office, and vibe shifts are short-lived. Biden's Democrats paid a price for ambitious legislating, and Trump will likely be punished for overreach.
forecasting_implication: Expect penalties for the president's party, e.g. a 2026 midterm penalty for the GOP.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
insight: Silver says Kamala Harris did not credibly run to the center in 2024. Her left-coded baggage from past campaigns persisted, and voters are skeptical of Etch-a-Sketch repositioning.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
insight: Voters rationally weigh competence, absence of scandal and adaptability alongside policy. Outsider status may carry a premium regardless of ideology (Osborn, Mamdani).

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
insight: Silver reports that 2024 nonvoters leaned Republican.
evidence: All studies, including the revised voter-file-validated CES (per Nate Cohn).
forecasting_implication: Higher turnout may not favor Democrats.

title: Is Susan Collins toast?
insight: Maine has moved left relative to the nation since 2016.
evidence: Maine was 0.9 points left of the nation in 2016, 4.6 in 2020 and 8.4 in 2024. It has voted left of the nation in every presidential election since 1988.
forecasting_implication: Recent-weighted partisan lean puts Maine at roughly D+8 relative to the nation.

title: Is Susan Collins toast?
insight: Democratic erosion in 2024 was concentrated in urban areas and among nonwhite voters. Rural white states like Maine and Vermont resisted the rightward trend, and that trend may have peaked.
evidence: Maine is the whitest state and the 6th-most rural.
forecasting_implication: Demographic composition should be used to model state-level swings.

title: Is Susan Collins toast?
insight: Ticket splitting has declined rapidly over the past decade, making it harder for crossover candidates like Collins and Tester to buck national trends.
evidence: Tester lost in 2024; candidate factors are becoming less predictive.
forecasting_implication: Shrink candidate-specific overperformance terms over time.

title: Is Susan Collins toast?
insight: In 2020 Collins won substantial crossover votes.
evidence: Exit polls show she won 38% of voters who thought abortion should be legal in all or most cases and 16% of those with an unfavorable view of Trump. She won 51% while Biden won 53% in Maine.

title: Is Susan Collins toast?
insight: Democrats need Maine plus one of Iowa, Texas, Florida, Alaska or Nebraska to retake the Senate. Without Maine they need two of those states.
evidence: Those states' 2024 margins ranged from R+13.2 to R+20.8. The seat-count table assumes Democrats win every state to the left of Minnesota.
forecasting_implication: State outcome correlation drives majority probability.
