title: Is Susan Collins toast?
insight: Maine's registered voters are 33% Democrats, 29% Republicans and 38% independents. The state has a tradition of ticket splitting and ranked-choice voting, and RCV is triggered only if no candidate wins a majority.
forecasting_implication: Ranked-choice voting tabulation may need to be modeled.

title: Is Susan Collins toast?
insight: In 2018, Democrats won the national House popular vote by about 7 points. The generic ballot average stood at D+3 in September 2025.
forecasting_implication: These figures give national-environment scenario values.

title: Actually, sometimes polls underestimate Democrats
insight: Polls struggle to reach low-propensity voters, those who vote in presidential races but skip midterms. Trump, and to a lesser extent Republicans generally, increasingly win this group, so presidential-year polls have underestimated Republicans while midterm polls, with high-propensity electorates, have been less biased.
evidence: Bias of D+3.0 in 2016, D+4.7 in 2020 and D+2.9 in 2024, versus D+0.8 in 2022 and R+0.5 in 2018.
forecasting_implication: Do not assume the presidential-year pro-Democratic poll bias carries over to midterms; consider bias priors specific to cycle type.

title: Actually, sometimes polls underestimate Democrats
insight: Pollsters disagree about whether the underestimation of Republicans is Trump-specific. Natalie Jackson's hypothesis is that Trump draws out voters who wouldn't turn out in a midterm, and possibly not for a different presidential candidate.
evidence: Quote from Natalie Jackson (GQR).
forecasting_implication: The direction of polling error may depend on whether Trump is on the ballot.

title: Actually, sometimes polls underestimate Democrats
insight: Democrats outperformed polls substantially in the 2025 New Jersey and Virginia governor's races, by about 9 and 6 points respectively. Mikie Sherrill in New Jersey was considerably underestimated.
evidence: Bias of R+9.0 in New Jersey and R+5.8 in Virginia.
forecasting_implication: This is a possible signal of Democratic strength under a Trump midterm environment, and of pollster overcorrection.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
insight: States like New Hampshire, with many independents and upper-middle-class suburban swing voters, respond more to national swings than polarized states like Mississippi, where voters are mostly firmly Democratic (largely Black voters) or firmly Republican (largely white evangelicals).
evidence: Elasticity estimates from CES microdata, 0.90 in Mississippi to 1.25 in Hawaii.
forecasting_implication: National swings should not be applied uniformly. Scale them by regional elasticity.

title: Midterm polls have good news, great news, and bad news for Democrats. Wait, what?
insight: The president's party usually loses ground in midterms. Exceptions such as 1998 (Lewinsky overreach) and 2002 (Sept. 11) are attributed to unusual events.
evidence: The opposition party won the House popular vote by 4.4 points on average since 1994.
forecasting_implication: Use a prior favoring the out-party in midterms.

title: Midterm polls have good news, great news, and bad news for Democrats. Wait, what?
insight: The out-party's generic ballot advantage tends to grow over the course of the midterm year.
evidence: Average gain of 2.5 points from late January to Election Day; it shrank only in 2018 and 2022.
forecasting_implication: Project drift toward the out-party in early-cycle forecasts.

title: Midterm polls have good news, great news, and bad news for Democrats. Wait, what?
insight: Democrats now benefit from low turnout because of their strength among highly engaged, college-educated voters.
evidence: The historical RV-to-LV shift toward Republicans has reversed.
forecasting_implication: LV adjustments should now favor Democrats rather than Republicans.

title: Midterm polls have good news, great news, and bad news for Democrats. Wait, what?
insight: Democrats' strong 2025 results were broadly consistent with an environment of about D+8.
evidence: A small sample of races; Democrats overperformed their polls.
forecasting_implication: Special and off-year elections can serve as a check on the national environment.

title: Midterm polls have good news, great news, and bad news for Democrats. Wait, what?
insight: Democrats recruited top Senate candidates for 2026 (Peltola in AK, Brown in OH, Cooper in NC). The authors contrast this with Republican candidate-quality problems in 2022.
forecasting_implication: Candidate quality could close benchmark gaps of 5-8 points.

title: Midterm polls have good news, great news, and bad news for Democrats. Wait, what?
insight: Trump's approval is near its second-term low of net −14, and second terms sometimes see the bottom fall out.
forecasting_implication: Approval may push the environment further toward the out-party.

title: Midterm polls have good news, great news, and bad news for Democrats. Wait, what?
insight: In wave elections, heavily gerrymandered seats can flip, turning gerrymanders into 'dummymanders', even though gerrymandering curbs the out-party's seat gains.
forecasting_implication: Seat translation should be nonlinear for large swings.

title: Midterm polls have good news, great news, and bad news for Democrats. Wait, what?
insight: Republicans won the House popular vote by 2.7 points in 2022 and 2.6 points in 2024.
forecasting_implication: Even a narrow R popular-vote win could cost Republicans their slim majority.

title: SBSQ #30: Will liberals turn against sports betting?
insight: Since 2012 California uses a top-two nonpartisan primary, which can produce perverse results such as two candidates of the same party advancing if the majority party's vote is split among many candidates.
evidence: March 2026 polls had two Republicans, Hilton and Bianco, leading individually while Democrats led combined 50.1 to 34.9.
forecasting_implication: Top-two primaries need candidate-level simulations with vote consolidation, not party-level averages.

title: SBSQ #30: Will liberals turn against sports betting?
insight: Opposition to sports betting is currently bipartisan, from religious conservatives and progressive paternalists, while the public is mostly indifferent; only 29 percent of Americans find gambling morally unacceptable per Pew.
evidence: State legalization map; California rejected sports betting initiatives in 2022 while Missouri narrowly approved one in 2024.

title: “AI polls” are fake polls
insight: Some voter types, for example young Black men who voted for Trump, are hard to reach in surveys, so their views are usually inferred rather than measured.
forecasting_implication: Subgroup shifts among hard-to-reach voters may be invisible to polls and models until results come in.

title: “AI polls” are fake polls
insight: In 2024 some Arizona and Nevada voters backed Trump and also voted to expand abortion rights on state ballot initiatives, a nuance pollsters doubt LLM agents can reproduce.
evidence: Comment from Natalie Jackson, GQR.

title: SBSQ #31: Trump is super unpopular. So why don’t Democrats have a bigger lead?
insight: Midterms are mostly about the president and the president's party, especially when it controls all levers of government; incumbency never helped the president's party in midterms and may be becoming a disadvantage even in presidential years.
forecasting_implication: Weight presidential approval heavily in the midterm national environment.

title: SBSQ #31: Trump is super unpopular. So why don’t Democrats have a bigger lead?
insight: Democratic voters' poor rating of their own party reflects anger at leadership, not despondency, and angry voters turn out; they will not defect to MAGA Republicans.
forecasting_implication: Low party favorability need not imply low turnout or vote share for the out-party.

title: SBSQ #31: Trump is super unpopular. So why don’t Democrats have a bigger lead?
insight: In 2018 Democrats gained 40 House seats but lost one Senate seat, largely because of a bad map.
forecasting_implication: Chamber outcomes depend on map composition, not just national environment.

title: Should Democrats panic about Platner?
insight: Maine has become bluer as recent transplants come overwhelmingly from Democratic-leaning groups: Clinton won by 3 points in 2016, Harris by 7 in 2024.
evidence: Presidential margins 2016 and 2024.
forecasting_implication: Partisan lean should weight recent elections more heavily.

title: Should Democrats panic about Platner?
insight: In 2020 Maine ticket-splitters may have backed Collins as a check on an expected Democratic president; with Trump in office in 2026 that motive is absent.
forecasting_implication: Incumbent overperformance can depend on which party holds the White House.

title: Should Democrats panic about Platner?
insight: A conventional candidate like Mills is a lower-variance bet, which is what a party wants in a blue state in a blue year.
forecasting_implication: Candidate uncertainty should widen outcome distributions.

title: Is the vibecession real — or is the survey broken?
insight: As Democrats soured on their own leadership, many Democratic-leaning voters began identifying as independents while still voting Democratic; Harris won independents in the 2024 national exit poll while losing the popular vote.
evidence: 2024 exit poll.
forecasting_implication: Party ID composition shifts can masquerade as opinion shifts among independents.

title: Is the vibecession real — or is the survey broken?
insight: Economic sentiment is now driven heavily by partisanship, with each side rating the economy far worse under the other party's president.
evidence: Michigan ICS by party, 2016-2026.
forecasting_implication: Sentiment-based economic indicators carry partisan bias and should be used cautiously as fundamentals.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
insight: Normal midterms are bad for the president's party, especially with an unpopular president; 2026 had approval near -20 net with only 22 percent strongly approving.
evidence: Trump net approval about -20 in August 2026.
forecasting_implication: Low strong-approval share signals turnout weakness for the president's party.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
insight: Polls underestimated Democrats in the November 2025 elections in Virginia and New Jersey, whose margins were consistent with a blue wave.
forecasting_implication: Off-year and special elections serve as leading indicators.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
insight: Despite DNC fundraising trouble, the top 7 Senate candidates in fundraising in 2026 were all Democrats.
forecasting_implication: Candidate-level fundraising matters more than party committee fundraising.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
insight: Silver believes the empirical evidence strongly points toward more moderate candidates being more electable.
forecasting_implication: Candidate ideology can enter as a fundamentals factor.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
insight: Party means in congressional voting (Voteview) have kept diverging, so the parties now vote as unified blocks with almost no crossover, and election outcomes increasingly follow partisanship.
evidence: Voteview party-mean difference.
forecasting_implication: Scale the weight on partisan lean versus candidate factors with a polarization index.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
insight: Gubernatorial races still feature much more ticket-splitting than congressional races, for example Republican Phil Scott in Vermont.
forecasting_implication: Use weaker partisan priors and wider uncertainty for governor races.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
insight: The 2018 midterm had pockets of Republican strength (Florida, rural Senate states) and 2022 had a mini red wave in New York and New Jersey.
forecasting_implication: Model regional and demographic correlated errors, not just national swing.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
insight: Susan Collins won Maine by 8.6 points in 2020 while Biden won it by 9.1, an extreme split-ticket overperformance.
evidence: 2020 results.
forecasting_implication: Some incumbents carry personal vote effects far beyond typical incumbency.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
insight: North Carolina has voted Democratic for president only once since 1976 (2008) and is often close-but-not-quite for Democrats, though it sits near the national median.

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
insight: The traditional Republican midterm turnout edge may have flipped to Democrats, because college graduates, now central to the Democratic coalition, vote at high rates in midterms.
evidence: In 2026 most paired LV/RV polls showed Democrats gaining in the LV version.
forecasting_implication: Reconsider the sign of likely-voter adjustment priors.

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
topic: Florida no longer a swing state
insight: Democrats largely wrote off Florida in 2026; FLIPR judged even Kansas a better reach state.

title: A tour of the 48 key House races
insight: Republicans pursued an unusual nationwide mid-decade redistricting push expecting to lose the House; Democratic states like California counteracted part of it.
forecasting_implication: District partisan leans must be recomputed on new boundaries each cycle.

title: A tour of the 48 key House races
insight: In 2026 Democratic upside was concentrated in the Northeast, Midwest and West, while redistricting handed Republicans seats in the South.

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
insight: Democrats last won Texas decisively for president in 1964 and have not won a Texas governor race since 1990 or Senate race since 1988; from 1952 to 1980 Texas was a key swing state, and it has never been liberal.
evidence: Historical results; McGovern lost Texas by 33 in 1972.
forecasting_implication: Long losing streaks are weak evidence once the environment and candidates change.

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
insight: After 2018, the Texas suburbs kept swinging blue but Democratic margins among working-class Hispanics in South and West Texas collapsed; a winning Democratic map needs both.
forecasting_implication: Demographic subgroup swings drive state outcomes and correlated errors.

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
insight: VP picks generally do not matter much electorally; LBJ in Texas in 1960 is an exception.

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
insight: Voters split tickets more for governor because control of a legislative chamber is not at stake; in Senate races, even voters who prefer the other party's candidate vote for chamber control.
evidence: Kansas has elected Democratic governors repeatedly but no Democratic senator since 1932.
forecasting_implication: Use weaker partisan priors for executive races.

title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
insight: The idea that voters only tune in after Labor Day is outdated; modern midterm environments change little after it.
evidence: 1.4-point average post-Labor Day generic ballot movement since 2010.
forecasting_implication: Shrink national drift variance in the fall of a midterm.

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
insight: Gas prices near $4.50 per gallon, up $1.29 in a year, with diesel up even more, coincided with Democratic polling gains in September 2026.
forecasting_implication: Fuel prices can be a salient economic fundamental.

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
insight: A D+8 to D+9 environment is about an 11-point swing from 2024, putting Ohio (Trump +11) at toss-up and Florida, Alaska, Iowa (Trump +13) and Texas (+14) near toss-up.
forecasting_implication: Uniform swing from the prior presidential baseline gives a quick map of the competitive field.

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
insight: In Trump's previous midterm (2018) Democrats won the House popular vote by 8.6 points.

title: Do Republicans really have a money advantage?
insight: In 2026 Republicans dominated party and Super PAC cash (MAGA Inc. alone $416M) while Democrats dominated candidate fundraising via grassroots platforms like ActBlue; the DNC itself was weak with $18M debt.
evidence: FEC filings through August 2026.
forecasting_implication: Party-committee finances are a poor proxy for candidate strength.

title: Do Republicans really have a money advantage?
insight: Democratic challengers in competitive House districts outraised GOP incumbents, consistent with an enthusiasm advantage.
evidence: Cook Political Report Q2 2026 analysis.
forecasting_implication: Challenger fundraising relative to incumbents signals wave conditions.

title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
insight: Midterm backsliding for the president's party is perhaps the most durable trend in American politics, driven by thermostatic opinion and perceived overreach (1946, 1966, 1974, 1994, 2010).
evidence: House popular vote swings since 1944.
forecasting_implication: A strong prior toward out-party gains is justified even without polls.

title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
insight: Before 1994, Democratic House dominance rested on a coalition of Northern liberals and Southern populists; realignments in 1972, 1980, 1994, 2010 and 2016 moved rural and Southern white voters to Republicans.
forecasting_implication: Pre-1994 House data reflect a different party system; weight recent data more.

title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
insight: Only four Republican senators hold true swing states, and the Senate's equal apportionment by state is what keeps Republican hopes alive in a strong Democratic year.
forecasting_implication: Senate outcomes depend heavily on which seats are up.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
insight: In the Trump era college-educated voters are more likely to answer polls and to vote Democratic, while non-college whites lean heavily Republican; failing to weight by education caused the 2016 Midwest miss.
forecasting_implication: Weight or model by education; expect correlated errors among non-college-heavy states.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
insight: Democrats have generally outperformed polls and expectations in Trump-era special and off-year elections.
evidence: 246 polls across 36 races since 2016.
forecasting_implication: Special elections are leading indicators but with independent, noisy errors.

title: Welcome to midterm silly season 🤡
insight: In mid-October 2026, gas prices came off their peak while oil futures rose again, inflation ran hot, and mortgage rates climbed.
forecasting_implication: Late economic news rarely moves an already-baked midterm environment much.

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
insight: Many Republicans in red states and districts had not faced a strong Democratic year since 2018, for example Roger Marshall in Kansas.
forecasting_implication: Incumbent strength measured in neutral years may overstate resilience in wave years.

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
insight: Unusually, reported Republican internal polling in October 2026 was nearly as bad for Republicans as public polling.
forecasting_implication: Leaked internals agreeing with public polls reduces the chance of a hidden bias.

title: My pet peeve about the polling error debate
insight: Explanations like 'polls underestimate Republicans in presidential years but not midterms' have some theoretical support (low-propensity Trump voters) but may be overfitting to noise.
evidence: Trump-year misses 2016, 2020, 2024; unbiased 2018, 2022; pro-R bias 2025.
forecasting_implication: Do not encode directional bias assumptions; model symmetric uncertainty.

title: Do these Senate-governor splits make sense?
insight: Nationalized politics make it increasingly hard to be a blue-state Republican or red-state Democrat, though governors (Scott in Vermont, Ayotte in New Hampshire, Kansas Democrats) still buck partisanship more than senators.
evidence: Median split fell from 25 (1990) to 8 (2022).
forecasting_implication: Shrink candidate-specific deviations over time; keep larger deviations for governors.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
insight: Predicted Democratic suburban gains in Texas were offset by Trump's gains with working-class Latinos in South Texas, which 2026 polls suggest may reverse.
forecasting_implication: Subgroup trend reversals can swing state baselines quickly.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
insight: Kansas is trending slightly blue relative to the nation (Clinton -21 in 2016, Harris -16 in 2024), with Democratic wins in KS-3, governor races and the 2022 abortion referendum.

title: The 83 remotely competitive House races, according to FLIPR
insight: Hispanic voters in South Texas appeared to be swinging back toward Democrats in 2026, putting Trump+18 TX-15 in play.
evidence: Pulido +8.2 in polling average.
forecasting_implication: Demographic group swings create correlated district-level shifts.

title: The 83 remotely competitive House races, according to FLIPR
insight: Mid-decade redistricting tilted the House map toward Republicans, but some redrawn seats could become 'dummymanders' in a large wave.

title: 13 maps for the morning after the midterms
insight: Bill Nelson's 2018 loss in Florida amid a blue wave, when Florida was only slightly right of the tipping point, presaged a Democratic death spiral in the state.
forecasting_implication: Anomalous results relative to the environment can signal durable realignment.

title: 13 maps for the morning after the midterms
insight: Alaska and Maine count slowly and use ranked-choice voting, so Senate control may not be known for days.

title: Where polls and fundamentals clash
insight: Candidate-quality overperformances are rarer than before but good or bad candidates can still move margins a few points, enough to decide Senate control in a close map.
evidence: Fancy vs simple fundamentals gaps in Texas, Ohio, Maine.
forecasting_implication: Keep a reduced but nonzero candidate-quality component.

title: It's Judgment Day for Trump (and for pollsters)
insight: Trump's ability to turn out low-propensity voters, who are often missed by polls, has not worked when he is not on the ballot.
evidence: Midterm and special election results in the Trump era.
forecasting_implication: Do not carry presidential-year R polling bias assumptions into midterms.

title: It's Judgment Day for Trump (and for pollsters)
insight: Most 2026 Senate winners serve six years spanning the whole next presidential term, giving parties strong incentives to limit losses, which revealed gloomy Republican internal assessments through defensive spending.
evidence: GOP spending in Texas, Nebraska, Louisiana.
forecasting_implication: Party spending patterns can signal private polling.
